![Watch Karpathy's talk on YouTube. [Watch on YouTube](https://youtu.be/LCEmiRjPEtQ)](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

[Andrej Karpathy](https://karpathy.ai/), former Director of AI and Autopilot Vision at [Tesla](https://www.tesla.com/), co-founding member of [OpenAI](https://openai.com/), and the man who coined ["vibe coding"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vibe_coding), gave a 40min talk on ["Software in the Era of AI"](https://youtu.be/LCEmiRjPEtQ):

- **[Software 3.0](#ch-software-evolution):** Programming in English. Three paradigms now coexist (1.0 code, 2.0 weights, 3.0 prompts), and it's worth being fluent in all three.
- **[LLMs as utilities, fabs, and operating systems](#ch-utilities-fabs-os):** metered intelligence over APIs (utility) and heavy centralizing capex (fab), but most of all a new operating system, with the LLM as the CPU and the context window as its memory.
- [Comparing current LLM evolution to 60s](#ch-llm-os) (mainframe era).
- [Cloud-first and on-device](#ch-llm-os): compute is still expensive, so intelligence is centralized and time-shared. On-device LLMs (e.g. on Mac minis) are only just emerging.
- **[Flipped technology diffusion](#ch-llm-os):** unlike electricity, computing, or the internet, LLMs reached billions of consumers first, ahead of governments and corporations.
- LLM is like ["fallible people spirits"](#ch-psychology): stochastic simulation of people, or I call "quantum state of personas" (prompting causing wave function collapse). Superhuman recall but jagged: hallucination, no persistent learning (anterograde amnesia), and gullible to prompt injection.
- [**"Autonomy slider"**](#ch-partial-autonomy) to meet LLMs half-way: partial autonomy apps — AI generates suggestions and humans verify them. Build [Iron Man suits](#ch-iron-man) (augmentation) over fully autonomous robots.
- **[Keep the AI on a leash](#ch-collaboration-loops):** the human is the bottleneck and verifier, so speed the generation–verification loop with GUIs and small, concrete diffs rather than 10,000-line dumps.
- **[Vibe coding](#ch-vibe-coding):** the human role shifts from coder to context-wrangler or orchestrator. Programming in English means everyone is now a programmer.
- **[Build systems for agents](#ch-build-for-agents):** clean and well-documented APIs for agents; robots.txt → llms.txt, docs in Markdown, "click" replaced with curl commands, and protocols like MCP.
- [2025–2035 will mark the "decade of agents"](#ch-tesla-autopilot), not the year: self-driving took 12+ years and still needs humans in the loop.

With help of AI, I've built an **[enriched transcript](#transcript) at the bottom of this post** — the talk's auto-captions, lightly edited and reorganized into chapters and subsections, with inline hyperlinks, acronym expansions, and editor's-note callouts. See the preamble of that section for details.

### [0:00:00 — Intro](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ&t=0s) {#ch-intro}

Please welcome former Director of AI [Tesla], Andrej Karpathy. [Applause] Wow, a lot of people here. Hello. Okay, yeah. So I'm excited to be here today to talk to you about software in the era of AI. And I'm told that many of you are students — bachelors, masters, PhD and so on — and you're about to enter the industry. And I think it's actually an extremely unique and very interesting time to enter the industry right now. And I think fundamentally the reason for that is that *software is changing again*.

And I say again because I actually gave this talk already. But the problem is that software keeps changing, so I actually have a lot of material to create new talks. And I think it's changing quite fundamentally. I think roughly speaking software has not changed much on such a fundamental level for 70 years, and then it's changed I think about twice quite rapidly in the last few years. And so there's just a huge amount of work to do, a huge amount of software to write and rewrite.

So let's take a look at the realm of software. If we think of this as the map of software, this is a really cool tool called [Map of GitHub](https://anvaka.github.io/map-of-github/). This is all the software that's written. These are instructions to the computer for carrying out tasks in the digital space.

### [0:01:25 — Software evolution: from 1.0 to 3.0](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ&t=85s) {#ch-software-evolution}

#### Software 1.0, 2.0, and the GitHub of weights

So if you zoom in here, these are all different kinds of repositories, and this is all the code that has been written. A few years ago I observed that software was changing and there was a new type of software around, and I called this [Software 2.0](https://karpathy.medium.com/software-2-0-a64152b37c35) at the time. The idea here was that Software 1.0 is the code you write for the computer. Software 2.0 are basically neural networks — and in particular the weights of a neural network. You're not writing this code directly; you are more kind of like tuning the data sets and then running an optimizer to create the parameters of this neural net.

At the time neural nets were kind of seen as just a different kind of classifier, like a decision tree or something like that, so I think this framing was a lot more appropriate now. What we have is the equivalent of GitHub in the realm of Software 2.0, and I think [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/) is basically the equivalent of GitHub in Software 2.0. And there's also Model Atlas, and you can visualize all the code written there. In case you're curious, the giant circle, the point in the middle — these are the parameters of [FLUX](https://blackforestlabs.ai/), the image generator. So anytime someone tunes on top of a FLUX model, you basically create a git commit in this space and you create a different kind of image generator.

So basically, Software 1.0 is the computer code that programs a computer. Software 2.0 are the weights which program neural networks. Here's an example of [AlexNet](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/4824-imagenet-classification-with-deep-convolutional-neural-networks) [[1]](#ref-1), an image-recognizer neural network.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** [AlexNet](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/4824-imagenet-classification-with-deep-convolutional-neural-networks) [[1]](#ref-1) is the 2012 ImageNet-winning convolutional network from Krizhevsky, Sutskever, and Hinton, widely credited with starting the modern deep-learning era.
:::

#### Software 3.0: prompts as programs in English

Now, so far all of the neural networks that we've been familiar with until recently were kind of like fixed-function computers: image to categories, or something like that. And what's changed — and I think this is a quite fundamental change — is that neural networks became programmable with [large language models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_language_model). So I see this as quite new and unique. It's a new kind of computer, and so in my mind it's worth giving it a new designation of Software 3.0. Basically your prompts are now programs that program the LLM, and remarkably these prompts are written in English. So it's a very interesting programming language.

To summarize the difference: if you're doing sentiment classification, for example, you can imagine writing some amount of Python to do sentiment classification, or you can train a neural net, or you can prompt a large language model. Here this is a few-shot prompt, and you can imagine changing it and programming the computer in a slightly different way. So we have Software 1.0, Software 2.0, and I think we're seeing — maybe you've seen — a lot of GitHub code is not just code anymore. There's a bunch of English interspersed with code, and so there's a growing category of a new kind of code.

So not only is it a new programming paradigm, it's also remarkable to me that it's in our native language of English. When this blew my mind a few — I guess years ago now — I tweeted this, and I think it captured the attention of a lot of people. This is my currently pinned tweet: that remarkably, *we're now programming computers in English*. Now, when I was at Tesla, we were working on the [Autopilot](https://www.tesla.com/autopilot) and we were trying to get the car to drive, and I sort of showed this slide at the time,

### [0:04:40 — Programming in English: the rise of Software 3.0](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ&t=280s) {#ch-programming-english}

where you can imagine that the inputs to the car are on the bottom, and they're going through a software stack to produce the steering and acceleration. I made the observation at the time that there was a ton of C++ code around in the Autopilot, which was the Software 1.0 code, and then there were some neural nets in there doing image recognition. And I observed that over time, as we made the Autopilot better, the neural network grew in capability and size, and in addition to that all the C++ code was being deleted. A lot of the capabilities and functionality that was originally written in 1.0 was migrated to 2.0.

As an example, a lot of the stitching up of information across images from the different cameras and across time was done by a neural network, and we were able to delete a lot of code. So the Software 2.0 stack quite literally ate through the software stack of the Autopilot. I thought this was really remarkable at the time, and I think we're seeing the same thing again, where we have a new kind of software and it's eating through the stack.

We have three completely different programming paradigms, and I think if you're entering the industry it's a very good idea to *be fluent in all of them*, because they all have slight pros and cons. You may want to program some functionality in 1.0 or 2.0 or 3.0. Are you going to train a neural net? Are you going to just prompt an LLM? Should this be a piece of code that's explicit? So we all have to make these decisions and potentially fluidly transition between these paradigms.

### [0:06:10 — LLMs as utilities, fabs, and operating systems](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ&t=370s) {#ch-utilities-fabs-os}

So what I wanted to get into now: first, I want to talk about LLMs and how to think of this new paradigm and the ecosystem, and what that looks like. What is this new computer? What does it look like, and what does the ecosystem look like?

#### LLMs as utilities

I was struck by this quote from [Andrew](https://www.andrewng.org/) actually, many years ago now — and I think Andrew is going to be speaking right after me. He said at the time, AI is the new electricity. I do think it captures something very interesting, in that LLMs certainly feel like they have properties of utilities right now. LLM labs like OpenAI, [Gemini](https://deepmind.google/technologies/gemini/), [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/) and so on spend capex [capital expenditure] to train the LLMs, and this is kind of equivalent to building out a grid. Then there's opex [operating expenditure] to serve that intelligence over APIs to all of us, and this is done through metered access where we pay per million tokens or something like that. And we have a lot of demands that are very utility-like out of this API: we demand low latency, high uptime, consistent quality, and so on.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The "AI is the new electricity" line is [Andrew Ng](https://www.andrewng.org/)'s; he began using it around 2017. Ng spoke at the same event right after Karpathy.
:::

In electricity, you would have a transfer switch, so you can transfer your electricity source from the grid, solar, battery, or generator. In LLMs, we have maybe [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/) and easily switch between the different types of LLMs that exist. Because the LLMs are software, they don't compete for physical space, so it's okay to have basically six electricity providers and you can switch between them, because they don't compete in such a direct way.

What's also a little fascinating — and we saw this in the last few days actually — a lot of the LLMs went down and people were kind of stuck and unable to work. It's fascinating to me that when the state-of-the-art LLMs go down, it's actually kind of like an *intelligence brownout* in the world. It's like when the voltage is unreliable in the grid, and the planet just gets dumber the more reliance we have on these models — which already is really dramatic, and I think will continue to grow.

#### LLMs as fabs

But LLMs don't only have properties of utilities. I think it's also fair to say that they have some properties of fabs. The reason for this is that the capex required for building LLMs is actually quite large. It's not just like building a power station; you're investing a huge amount of money, and the tech tree for the technology is growing quite rapidly. So we're in a world where we have deep tech trees, research and development secrets that are centralizing inside the LLM labs.

But I think the analogy muddies a little bit also because, as I mentioned, this is software, and software is a bit less defensible because it is so malleable. There are many analogies you can make: a 4-nanometer process node maybe is something like a cluster with certain max flops [floating-point operations]. When you're using [Nvidia](https://www.nvidia.com/) GPUs and you're only doing the software and not the hardware, that's kind of like the fabless model. But if you're actually also building your own hardware and you're training on [TPUs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_Processing_Unit) [tensor processing units] if you're Google, that's kind of like the Intel model where you own your fab.

#### LLMs as operating systems

But actually I think the analogy that makes the most sense perhaps is that, in my mind, *LLMs have very strong analogies to operating systems*. This is not just electricity or water. It's not something that comes out of the tap as a commodity. These are now increasingly complex software ecosystems. It's kind of interesting to me that the ecosystem is shaping up in a very similar way, where you have a few closed-source providers like Windows or macOS, and then you have an open-source alternative like Linux. For LLMs as well, we have a few competing closed-source providers, and then maybe the [Llama](https://www.llama.com/) ecosystem is currently a close approximation to something that may grow into something like Linux. I think it's still very early, because these are just simple LLMs, but we're starting to see that these are going to get a lot more complicated. It's not just about the LLM itself; it's about all the tool use and the multimodalities and how all of that works.

So when I had this realization a while back, I tried to sketch it out, and it seemed to me like LLMs are kind of like a new operating system. The LLM is a new kind of computer — it's the CPU equivalent. The context windows are kind of like the memory, and then the LLM is orchestrating memory and compute for problem solving using all of these capabilities. So it looks very much like an operating system from that perspective.

A few more analogies. If you want to download an app — say I go to [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/) and download it — you can run it on Windows, Linux, or Mac, in the same way as you can take an LLM app like [Cursor](https://cursor.com/) and run it on GPT, Claude, or the Gemini series. It's just a dropdown. So it's similar in that way as well.

### [0:11:04 — The new LLM OS and historical computing analogies](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ&t=664s) {#ch-llm-os}

#### The 1960s time-sharing era

More analogies that strike me: we're kind of in this 1960s-ish era where LLM compute is still very expensive for this new kind of computer, and that forces the LLMs to be centralized in the cloud. We're all just thin clients that interact with it over the network, and none of us have full utilization of these computers. Therefore it makes sense to use [time sharing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time-sharing), where we're all just a dimension of the batch when they're running the computer in the cloud. This is very much what computers used to look like during this time: the operating systems were in the cloud, everything was streamed around, and there was batching.

The personal computing revolution hasn't happened yet because it's just not economical — it doesn't make sense. But some people are trying. It turns out that [Mac minis](https://www.apple.com/mac-mini/), for example, are a very good fit for some of the LLMs, because if you're doing batch-one inference, this is all super memory-bound, so this actually works. These are some early indications maybe of personal computing, but this hasn't really happened yet. It's not clear what this looks like. Maybe some of you get to invent what this is, or how it works, or what it should be.

Maybe one more analogy I'll mention: whenever I talk to [ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/) or some LLM directly in text, I feel like I'm talking to an operating system through the terminal. It's just text. It's direct access to the operating system. And I think a [GUI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphical_user_interface) [graphical user interface] hasn't yet really been invented in a general way. Should ChatGPT have a GUI different from just text bubbles? Certainly some of the apps that we're going to go into in a bit have a GUI, but there's no GUI across all the tasks, if that makes sense.

#### Flipped technology diffusion

There are some ways in which LLMs are different from operating systems in a fairly unique way, and from early computing. I wrote about this one particular property that strikes me as very different this time around: LLMs flip the direction of technology diffusion that is usually present in technology. For example, with electricity, cryptography, computing, flight, internet, GPS — lots of new transformative technologies that have not been around — typically it is the government and corporations that are the first users, because it's new and expensive, and it only later diffuses to the consumer.

But I feel like LLMs are kind of flipped around. Maybe with early computers it was all about ballistics and military use, but with LLMs, it's all about how do you boil an egg or something like that. This is certainly a lot of my use. So it's really fascinating to me that we have a new magical computer and it's helping me boil an egg. It's not helping the government do something really crazy like military ballistics or some special technology. Indeed, corporations and governments are lagging behind the adoption of all of us, of all of these technologies. So it's just backwards, and I think it informs some of the uses of how we want to use this technology, or where are some of the first apps.

So in summary so far: LLM labs make LLMs, but LLMs are complicated operating systems. They're circa 1960s in computing, and we're redoing computing all over again. They're currently available via time sharing and distributed like a utility. What is new and unprecedented is that they're not in the hands of a few governments and corporations — *they're in the hands of all of us*, because we all have a computer, and it's all just software. ChatGPT was beamed down to our computers, like billions of people, instantly and overnight, and this is insane. It's kind of insane to me that this is the case. Now it is our time to enter the industry and program these computers. This is crazy.

### [0:14:39 — Psychology of LLMs: people spirits and cognitive quirks](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ&t=879s) {#ch-psychology}

#### People spirits: stochastic simulations of people

So I think this is quite remarkable. Before we program LLMs, we have to spend some time to think about what these things are. And I especially like to talk about their psychology. The way I like to think about LLMs is that they're kind of like people spirits. They are stochastic simulations of people, and the simulator in this case happens to be an [autoregressive transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) [[2]](#ref-2). The transformer is a neural net, and it just goes on the level of tokens — chunk, chunk, chunk, chunk — and there's an almost equal amount of compute for every single chunk. This simulator, of course, has some weights involved, and we fit it to all of the text that we have on the internet and so on. You end up with this kind of simulator, and because it is trained on humans, it's got this emergent psychology that is humanlike.

#### Encyclopedic memory — the Rain Man comparison

The first thing you'll notice, of course, is that LLMs have encyclopedic knowledge and memory. They can remember lots of things, a lot more than any single individual human can, because they read so many things. It actually reminds me of this movie [Rain Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain_Man), which I really recommend people watch. It's an amazing movie, I love it. Dustin Hoffman here is an autistic savant who has almost perfect memory, so he can read a phone book and remember all of the names and phone numbers. I feel like LLMs are very similar — they can remember SHA hashes and lots of different kinds of things very, very easily. So they certainly have superpowers in some respects.

#### Jagged intelligence and hallucination

But they also have a bunch of what I would say are cognitive deficits. They hallucinate quite a bit, and they make up stuff and don't have a very good internal model of self-knowledge — not sufficient, at least. This has gotten better but not perfect. They display *jagged intelligence*: they're going to be superhuman in some problem-solving domains, and then they're going to make mistakes that basically no human will make. They will insist that 9.11 is greater than 9.9, or that there are two R's in "strawberry" — these are some famous examples. But basically there are rough edges that you can trip on.

#### Anterograde amnesia and working memory

They also kind of suffer from [anterograde amnesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anterograde_amnesia). I'm alluding to the fact that if you have a co-worker who joins your organization, this co-worker will over time learn your organization and gain a huge amount of context on it. They go home and they sleep and they consolidate knowledge, and they develop expertise over time. LLMs don't natively do this, and this is not something that has really been solved in the R&D of LLMs. Context windows are really kind of like working memory, and you have to program the working memory quite directly, because they don't just get smarter by default. A lot of people get tripped up by the analogies in this way.

In popular culture I recommend people watch these two movies, [Memento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memento_(film)) and [50 First Dates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/50_First_Dates). In both of these movies the protagonists' weights are fixed and their context windows get wiped every single morning, and it's really problematic to go to work or have relationships when this happens.

#### Security: gullibility and prompt injection

One more thing I would point to is security-related limitations of the use of LLMs. For example, LLMs are quite gullible. They are susceptible to [prompt injection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prompt_injection) risks, they might leak your data, and there are many other security-related considerations. So basically, long story short, you have to simultaneously think through this superhuman thing that has a bunch of cognitive deficits and issues. How do we program them, work around their deficits, and enjoy their superhuman powers?

### [0:18:22 — Designing LLM apps with partial autonomy](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ&t=1102s) {#ch-partial-autonomy}

So what I want to switch to now is the opportunities — how do we use these models, and what are some of the biggest opportunities? This is not a comprehensive list, just some of the things I thought were interesting for this talk.

#### Cursor as the model LLM app

The first thing I'm excited about is what I would call partial autonomy apps. Let's work with the example of coding. You can certainly go to ChatGPT directly and start copy-pasting code around, and copy-pasting bug reports, and getting code and copy-pasting everything around. Why would you do that? Why would you go directly to the operating system? It makes a lot more sense to have an app dedicated for this. Many of you use [Cursor](https://cursor.com/) — I do as well — and Cursor is the thing you want instead. You don't want to just directly go to the ChatGPT app. I think Cursor is a very good example of an early LLM app that has a bunch of properties useful across all the LLM apps.

#### The shared properties of LLM apps

In particular, you'll notice we have a traditional interface that allows a human to go in and do all the work manually, just as before. But in addition to that, we now have this LLM integration that allows us to go in bigger chunks. Some of the properties of LLM apps that I think are shared and useful to point out:

Number one, the LLMs basically do a ton of the context management. Number two, they orchestrate multiple calls to LLMs. In the case of Cursor, there are under the hood embedding models for all your files, the actual chat models, models that apply diffs to the code, and this is all orchestrated for you.

A really big one that maybe is not fully appreciated always is application-specific GUI and the importance of it. You don't just want to talk to the operating system directly in text. Text is very hard to read, interpret, and understand, and you don't want to take some of these actions natively in text. It's much better to just see a diff as a red and green change, where you can see what's being added and subtracted. It's much easier to just do Command-Y to accept or Command-N to reject. I shouldn't have to type it in text. So a GUI allows a human to audit the work of these fallible systems and to go faster.

#### The autonomy slider

The last feature I want to point out is what I call the autonomy slider. For example, in Cursor, you can just do tab completion — you're mostly in charge. You can select a chunk of code and Command-K to change just that chunk. You can do Command-L to change the entire file. Or you can do Command-I, which just lets it rip, do whatever you want in the entire repo — that's the full-autonomy agentic version. So you are in charge of the autonomy slider, and depending on the complexity of the task at hand, you can tune the amount of autonomy that you're willing to give up for that task.

Maybe to show one more example of a fairly successful LLM app: [Perplexity](https://www.perplexity.ai/). It also has very similar features to what I've pointed out in Cursor. It packages up a lot of the information, it orchestrates multiple LLMs, and it's got a GUI that allows you to audit some of its work — for example, it will cite sources and you can inspect them. And it's got an autonomy slider: you can either do a quick search, or you can do research, or you can do deep research and come back 10 minutes later. So this is all just varying levels of autonomy that you give up to the tool.

So I feel like a lot of software will become partially autonomous, and I'm trying to think through what that looks like. For many of you who maintain products and services: how are you going to make your products and services partially autonomous? Can an LLM see everything that a human can see? Can an LLM act in all the ways that a human could act? And can humans supervise and stay in the loop of this activity? Because again, these are fallible systems that aren't yet perfect. What does a diff look like in [Photoshop](https://www.adobe.com/products/photoshop.html) or something like that? A lot of traditional software right now has all these switches and all this kind of stuff that's all designed for humans, and all of this has to change and become accessible to LLMs.

#### Generation and verification — keeping the AI on the leash

One thing I want to stress with a lot of these LLM apps, which I'm not sure gets as much attention as it should, is that we're now cooperating with AIs. Usually they are doing the generation and we as humans are doing the verification. It is in our interest to make this loop go as fast as possible, so we're getting a lot of work done. There are two major ways this can be done.

Number one, you can speed up verification a lot. GUIs, for example, are extremely important to this, because a GUI utilizes your computer-vision GPU in all of our heads. Reading text is effortful and it's not fun, but looking at stuff is fun, and it's just a highway to your brain. So GUIs are very useful for auditing systems, and visual representations in general.

Number two, we have to keep the AI on the leash. A lot of people are getting way over-excited with AI agents, and it's not useful to me to get a diff of 10,000 lines of code to my repo. Even though those 10,000 lines come out instantly, I have to make sure that this thing is not introducing bugs, and that it's doing the correct thing, and that there are no security issues. So *I'm still the bottleneck*. So it's in our interest to make the flow of these two go very, very fast, and we have to somehow keep the AI on the leash because it gets way too overreactive. This is how I feel when I do AI-assisted coding: if I'm just vibe coding, everything is nice and great, but if I'm actually trying to get work done, it's not so great to have an overreactive agent doing all this kind of stuff.

### [0:23:40 — The importance of human–AI collaboration loops](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ&t=1420s) {#ch-collaboration-loops}

#### Small diffs, fast loops, concrete prompts

So this slide is not very good, I'm sorry, but I'm trying to develop — like many of you — some ways of utilizing these agents in my coding workflow and doing AI-assisted coding. In my own work, I'm always scared to get way too big diffs. I always go in small incremental chunks. I want to make sure that everything is good. I want to spin this loop very, very fast, and I work on small chunks of a single concrete thing. I think many of you probably are developing similar ways of working with LLMs.

I also saw a number of blog posts that try to develop these best practices for working with LLMs. Here's one that I read recently and thought was quite good. It discussed some techniques, and some of them have to do with how you keep the AI on the leash. As an example, if your prompt is vague, then the AI might not do exactly what you wanted, and in that case verification will fail. You're going to ask for something else, and if verification fails, you're going to start spinning. So it makes a lot more sense to spend a bit more time to be more concrete in your prompts, which increases the probability of successful verification and you can move forward.

#### Education: a teacher app and a student app

In my own work as well, I'm currently interested in what education looks like now that we have AI and LLMs. A large amount of thought for me goes into how we keep the AI on the leash. I don't think it just works to go to ChatGPT and be like, "Hey, teach me physics." I don't think this works because *the AI gets lost in the woods*. So for me, this is actually two separate apps. There's an app for a teacher that creates courses, and then there's an app that takes courses and serves them to students. In both cases, we now have this intermediate artifact of a course that is auditable, and we can make sure it's good and consistent, and the AI is kept on the leash with respect to a certain syllabus, a certain progression of projects. This is one way of keeping the AI on the leash, and I think it has a much higher likelihood of working, and the AI is not getting lost in the woods.

### [0:26:00 — Lessons from Tesla Autopilot and autonomy sliders](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ&t=1560s) {#ch-tesla-autopilot}

One more analogy I wanted to allude to: I'm no stranger to partial autonomy. I worked on this for five years at Tesla, and this is also a partial autonomy product that shares a lot of the features. For example, right there in the instrument panel is the GUI of the Autopilot — it's showing me what the neural network sees. And we have the autonomy slider, where over the course of my tenure there we did more and more autonomous tasks for the user.

Maybe the story I wanted to tell very briefly: the first time I drove a self-driving vehicle was in 2013. I had a friend who worked at [Waymo](https://waymo.com/), and he offered to give me a drive around Palo Alto. I took this picture using [Google Glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Glass) at the time — many of you are so young that you might not even know what that is, but this was all the rage at the time. We got into this car and went for about a 30-minute drive around Palo Alto highways, streets and so on, and this drive was perfect. There were zero interventions, and this was 2013, which is now 12 years ago.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** [Waymo](https://waymo.com/) didn't exist under that name in 2013 — it was then Google's self-driving car project and only spun out as Waymo in December 2016. The 2013 Palo Alto ride would have been in a Google car.
:::

It struck me, because at the time when I had this perfect drive, this perfect demo, I felt like, "Wow, self-driving is imminent, because this just worked. This is incredible." But here we are 12 years later, and we are still working on autonomy. We are still working on driving agents, and even now we haven't actually really solved the problem. You may see Waymos going around and they look driverless, but there's still a lot of teleoperation and a lot of human in the loop of a lot of this driving. So we still haven't even declared success, but I think it's definitely going to succeed at this point — it just took a long time.

So I think software is really tricky, in the same way that driving is tricky. When I see things like "Oh, 2025 is the year of agents," I get very concerned, and I feel like — you know — *this is the decade of agents*. This is going to be quite some time. We need humans in the loop. We need to do this carefully. This is software. Let's be serious here.

### [0:27:52 — The Iron Man analogy: augmentation vs. agents](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ&t=1672s) {#ch-iron-man}

One more analogy that I always think through is the [Iron Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Man) suit. I always love Iron Man — I think it's so correct in a bunch of ways with respect to technology and how it will play out. What I love about the Iron Man suit is that it's both an augmentation — Tony Stark can drive it — and it's also an agent. In some of the movies the Iron Man suit is quite autonomous and can fly around and find Tony and all this kind of stuff. So this is the autonomy slider: we can build augmentations, or we can build agents, and we kind of want to do a bit of both.

But at this stage, I would say, working with fallible LLMs and so on, it's *less Iron Man robots and more Iron Man suits* that you want to build. It's less like building flashy demos of autonomous agents, and more building partial autonomy products. These products have custom GUIs and UI/UX, and this is done so that the generation-verification loop of the human is very, very fast. But we are not losing sight of the fact that it is in principle possible to automate this work. There should be an autonomy slider in your product, and you should be thinking about how you can slide that autonomy slider and make your product more autonomous over time. So that's how I think there are lots of opportunities in these kinds of products.

### [0:29:06 — Vibe coding: everyone is now a programmer](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ&t=1746s) {#ch-vibe-coding}

#### The tweet that became a meme

I want to now switch gears a little bit and talk about one other dimension that I think is very unique. Not only is there a new type of programming language that allows for autonomy in software, but also, as I mentioned, it's programmed in English, which is this natural interface. Suddenly *everyone is a programmer*, because everyone speaks natural language like English. This is extremely bullish and very interesting to me, and also completely unprecedented. It used to be the case that you needed to spend five to 10 years studying something to be able to do something in software. This is not the case anymore.

So I don't know if by any chance anyone has heard of vibe coding. This is the tweet that introduced this, but I'm told that this is now like a major meme. Fun story about this: I've been on Twitter for like 15 years or something at this point, and I still have no clue which tweet will become viral and which tweet fizzles and no one cares. I thought that this tweet was going to be the latter — it was just like a shower thought. But this became a total meme, and I really just can't tell. I guess it struck a chord and it gave a name to something that everyone was feeling but couldn't quite say in words. So now there's a Wikipedia page and everything. [Applause] Yeah, this is like a major contribution now or something.

#### Vibe coding an iOS app and MenuGen

So Tom Wolf from [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/) shared this beautiful video that I really love. I find that this is such a wholesome video. How can you look at this video and feel bad about the future? The future is great. I think this will end up being like a gateway drug to software development. I'm not a doomer about the future of the generation.

So I tried vibe coding a little bit as well, because it's so fun. Vibe coding is so great when you want to build something super-duper custom that doesn't appear to exist, and you just want to wing it because it's a Saturday or something. I built this iOS app, and I can't actually program in [Swift](https://www.swift.org/), but I was really shocked that I was able to build a super basic app. I'm not going to explain it — it's really dumb — but this was just a day of work, and it was running on my phone later that day, and I was like, "Wow, this is amazing." I didn't have to read through Swift for five days to get started.

I also vibe coded this app called [MenuGen](https://menugen.app/). This is live — you can try it at menugen.app. I basically had this problem where I show up at a restaurant, I read through the menu, and I have no idea what any of the things are. I need pictures, and this doesn't exist, so I was like, "Hey, I'm going to vibe code it." So you go to menugen.app, you take a picture of a menu, and then MenuGen generates the images. Everyone gets $5 in credits for free when you sign up, and therefore this is a major cost center in my life. So this is a negative-revenue app for me right now — I've lost a huge amount of money on MenuGen.

#### The hard part wasn't the code — it was DevOps

But the fascinating thing about MenuGen for me is that the vibe-coding part — the code — was actually the easy part. Most of it was when I tried to make it real, so that you can actually have authentication and payments and the domain name and Vercel deployment. This was really hard, and all of this was not code. All of this DevOps stuff was me in the browser clicking stuff, and this took another week. So it was fascinating that I had the MenuGen demo working on my laptop in a few hours, and then it took me a week because I was trying to make it real, and the reason is this was just really annoying.

For example, if you try to add Google login to your web page, there's a huge amount of instructions from this [Clerk](https://clerk.com/) library telling me how to integrate this. And this is crazy — it's telling me to go to this URL, click on this dropdown, choose this, go to this, and click on that. A computer is telling me the actions I should be taking. Like, you do it! Why am I doing this? What the hell? I had to follow all these instructions. This was crazy.

### [0:33:39 — Building for agents: future-ready digital infrastructure](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ&t=2019s) {#ch-build-for-agents}

#### A new consumer of digital information

So the last part of my talk therefore focuses on: can we just build for agents? I don't want to do this work — can agents do this? Thank you. [Applause]

So roughly speaking, I think there's a new category of consumer and manipulator of digital information. It used to be just humans through GUIs, or computers through APIs. And now we have a completely new thing. Agents are computers, but they are humanlike — they're people spirits. There are people spirits on the internet, and they need to interact with our software infrastructure. Can we build for them? It's a new thing.

#### llms.txt and docs written for LLMs

As an example, you can have [robots.txt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robots.txt) on your domain, and you can instruct — or advise, I suppose — web crawlers on how to behave on your website. In the same way, you can have maybe an [llms.txt](https://llmstxt.org/) file, which is just a simple Markdown that's telling LLMs what this domain is about, and this is very readable to an LLM. If it had to instead get the HTML of your web page and try to parse it, this is very error-prone and difficult, and it's going to screw it up and it's not going to work. So we can just directly speak to the LLM. It's worth it.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** [`llms.txt`](https://llmstxt.org/) is a convention proposed by Jeremy Howard in 2024, not an established standard like [`robots.txt`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robots.txt). It's a single Markdown file at a site's root that tells an LLM what the site is about.
:::

A huge amount of documentation is currently written for people, so you'll see things like lists and bold and pictures, and this is not directly accessible by an LLM. So I see some of the services now transitioning a lot of their docs to be specifically for LLMs. [Vercel](https://vercel.com/) and [Stripe](https://stripe.com/) as an example are early movers here, but there are a few more I've seen already, and they offer their documentation in Markdown. Markdown is super easy for LLMs to understand. This is great.

Maybe one simple example from my own experience: maybe some of you know [3Blue1Brown](https://www.3blue1brown.com/). He makes beautiful animation videos on YouTube — I love this library. He wrote [Manim](https://www.manim.community/), and I wanted to make my own. There's extensive documentation on how to use Manim, and I didn't want to actually read through it, so I copy-pasted the whole thing to an LLM and described what I wanted, and it just worked out of the box. The LLM just vibe-coded me an animation, exactly what I wanted, and I was like, "Wow, this is amazing." So if we can make docs legible to LLMs, it's going to unlock a huge amount of use, and I think this is wonderful and should happen more.

#### Replacing "click" with curl, and the Model Context Protocol

The other thing I wanted to point out is that, unfortunately, it's not just about taking your docs and making them appear in Markdown — that's the easy part. We actually have to change the docs, because anytime your docs say "click," this is bad. An LLM will not be able to natively take this action right now. So Vercel, for example, is replacing every occurrence of "click" with an equivalent curl command that your LLM agent could take on your behalf. I think this is very interesting.

And then of course there's the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) from Anthropic. This is also another way — it's a protocol of speaking directly to agents as this new consumer and manipulator of digital information. So I'm very bullish on these ideas.

#### URL-swap tools: gitingest and DeepWiki

The other thing I really like is a number of little tools here and there that are helping ingest data in very LLM-friendly formats. For example, when I go to a GitHub repo like my [nanoGPT](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT) repo, I can't feed this to an LLM and ask questions about it, because it's a human interface on GitHub. But when you just change the URL from GitHub to [gitingest](https://gitingest.com/), this will actually concatenate all the files into a single giant text, and it will create a directory structure, and this is ready to be copy-pasted into your favorite LLM.

Maybe an even more dramatic example of this is [DeepWiki](https://deepwiki.com/), where it's not just the raw content of these files — this is from [Devin](https://devin.ai/), but they have Devin do analysis of the GitHub repo, and Devin basically builds up whole docs pages just for your repo, and you can imagine that this is even more helpful to copy-paste into your LLM. So I love all the little tools where you just change the URL and it makes something accessible to an LLM. This is all well and great, and I think there should be a lot more of it.

#### Meeting LLMs halfway

One more note I wanted to make: it is absolutely possible that in the future LLMs will be able to — this is not even future, this is today — go around and click stuff and so on. But I still think it's very worth *meeting LLMs halfway* and making it easier for them to access all this information, because this is still fairly expensive to use, and a lot more difficult. I do think that for lots of software there will be a long tail where it won't adapt, because these are not live, actively maintained repositories or digital infrastructure, and we will need these tools. But I think for everyone else, it's very worth meeting in some middle point. So I'm bullish on both, if that makes sense.

### [0:38:14 — Summary: we're in the 1960s of LLMs — time to build](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ&t=2294s) {#ch-summary}

So in summary, what an amazing time to get into the industry. We need to rewrite a ton of code. A ton of code will be written by professionals and by coders. These LLMs are kind of like utilities, kind of like fabs, but they're especially like operating systems. But it's so early — it's like the 1960s of operating systems — and I think a lot of the analogies cross over. These LLMs are kind of like these fallible people spirits that we have to learn to work with, and in order to do that properly, we need to adjust our infrastructure towards it.

So when you're building these LLM apps, I described some of the ways of working effectively with these LLMs, and some of the tools that make that possible, and how you can spin this loop very, very quickly and basically create partial autonomy products. And then a lot of code has to also be written for the agents more directly. But in any case, going back to the Iron Man suit analogy, I think what we'll see over the next decade roughly is that we're going to *take the slider from left to right*. And it's going to be very interesting to see what that looks like. And I can't wait to build it with all of [you].
